history.heading: From the Belgae to the Burgundian Netherlands
paragraphs: The name Belgium comes from the Belgae, Celtic tribes described by Julius Caesar as the bravest of the Gauls. The region was part of the Roman Empire and later the heartland of the Frankish kingdom; Charlemagne's family had its roots in the area around Liège.

In the Middle Ages, Flemish cities such as Bruges, Ghent and Ypres became some of the richest in Europe through the cloth trade. In the 14th and 15th centuries the Dukes of Burgundy united the Low Countries, and the region flourished as a centre of art and commerce, with painters such as Jan van Eyck.

history.heading: Spanish, Austrian and French rule
paragraphs: Through inheritance the Low Countries passed to the Habsburgs. Charles V was born in Ghent in 1500. The revolt against Spanish rule in the 16th century split the region: the northern provinces became the independent Dutch Republic, while the south, roughly modern Belgium, remained under Spain and then Austria.

Antwerp, one of Europe's greatest ports in the 16th century, declined after the split. The region was annexed by revolutionary France in 1795. After Napoleon's final defeat at Waterloo, just south of Brussels, in 1815, it was joined to the United Kingdom of the Netherlands.

history.heading: An independent kingdom
paragraphs: The Belgian Revolution of 1830 led to independence, and in 1831 Leopold of Saxe-Coburg became the first King of the Belgians. Belgium was the first country in continental Europe to industrialise, based on coal and steel in Wallonia.

King Leopold II ruled the Congo Free State as his personal possession from 1885 to 1908, a regime of forced labour and atrocities that killed millions of people. Belgium then governed the Congo as a colony until 1960, as well as Rwanda and Burundi until 1962.

history.heading: World wars and modern Belgium
paragraphs: Despite its neutrality, Belgium was invaded by Germany in both world wars. The battlefields of Flanders, including Ypres, saw some of the worst fighting of the First World War.

After 1945 Belgium was a founding member of the European communities and NATO. Tensions between Dutch-speaking Flanders and French-speaking Wallonia led to a series of state reforms from 1970, transforming Belgium into a federal state in 1993.

culture.heading: Languages and communities
paragraphs: Belgium has three official languages: Dutch, spoken in Flanders in the north; French, spoken in Wallonia in the south; and German, spoken by a small community in the east. Brussels is officially bilingual French and Dutch, though French is most widely used, and it is highly international.
Most Belgians are Catholic by tradition, though religious practice has declined sharply. Brussels and other cities have large communities of Moroccan, Turkish, Congolese and other origins.

culture.heading: Art and comics
paragraphs: Belgium has a rich artistic heritage, from the Flemish Primitives and Pieter Bruegel the Elder to Peter Paul Rubens and Anthony van Dyck, and later the surrealist René Magritte and the expressionist James Ensor. Victor Horta pioneered Art Nouveau architecture in Brussels.

The country is a capital of comics (bande dessinée): Hergé's Tintin, the Smurfs, Lucky Luke and Spirou are Belgian creations. Famous Belgians also include the singer Jacques Brel and the writer Georges Simenon.

culture.heading: Food, beer and festivals
paragraphs: Belgium is famous for chocolate, waffles, mussels with fries, and its fries (frites), often served from a frietkot. Belgian beer culture, with hundreds of styles including Trappist beers brewed by monks, is recognised by UNESCO.

Carnival traditions such as the Gilles of Binche are celebrated. Cycling is a passion, with classic races such as the Tour of Flanders, and Eddy Merckx is considered one of the greatest cyclists ever. Football is also hugely popular.

politics.heading: A complex federal state
paragraphs: Belgium is a federal parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy; the King of the Belgians has a largely ceremonial role. The federal level shares power with three regions (Flanders, Wallonia and Brussels-Capital) and three language communities (Flemish, French and German-speaking), each with its own parliament and government.

Political parties are split along language lines, so forming a federal government requires coalitions across both communities, which can take a very long time; after the 2010 election, it took 541 days. In Flanders, nationalist parties seeking more autonomy or independence are strong.

politics.heading: Heart of Europe
paragraphs: Brussels hosts the main institutions of the European Union, including the European Commission and the Council, as well as NATO headquarters, earning it the nickname "capital of Europe". Belgium was a founding member of the EU, NATO and the Benelux union with the Netherlands and Luxembourg.

economy.heading: An open economy
paragraphs: Belgium has a highly developed, open economy at the heart of Europe's main trade routes. The Port of Antwerp-Bruges is one of the largest ports in Europe, and Antwerp is a world centre of the diamond trade. Key industries include chemicals, pharmaceuticals, food processing, logistics and services.
Most trade is with neighbouring EU countries. The currency is the euro.

economy.heading: Regional differences and challenges
paragraphs: Wallonia was an early industrial powerhouse but suffered from the decline of coal and steel, while Flanders became more prosperous from the second half of the 20th century, which feeds political tensions. Brussels is a major services hub.

Belgium has high wages and productivity, a generous welfare system and some of the highest taxes on labour in the world. Challenges include high public debt, pension costs and relatively low employment rates in some regions.
